coredata.dc:description: The development of an environmentally safe soybean-based adhesive with desired adhesion properties and technological applicabilities, but low cost, still remains a challenge. In this study, a facile and clean strategy was developed to improve the adhesion properties and technological applicabilities and to reduce the cost of a soybean meal flour (SMF)-based adhesive through organic-inorganic hybridization with kaolin powder. The effects of kaolin hybridization and kaolin content on the structure and properties of the SMF-based adhesive were revealed. The improved water resistance of the adhesion was attributed to the effective organic-inorganic hybridization of the SMF adhesive with a uniform distribution of kaolin, the hydrogen bonding interactions between the intercalated SMF with the partial kaolin interlayers, and the chemical reaction between the crosslinker and kaolin. In addition, kaolin significantly decreased the viscosity and alleviated the shear thinning characteristics of the SMF adhesive because the kaolin-kaolin intermolecular interactions were weaker than the interactions between the SMF chains. Hydrogen bonding interactions between the SMF chains and the kaolin particles were observed, and the water absorption and bonded water by kaolin were greatly reduced. The most preferable kaolin content in the SMF adhesive was 30%, which decreased the adhesive cost by 11.4%. Thus, this novel strategy could effectively expand the applications of SMF-based adhesives in environmentally friendly wood composites by replacing formaldehyde-based synthetic resins that release free formaldehyde.

head.ce:title: Effect of kaolin content on the performances of kaolin-hybridized soybean meal-based adhesives for wood composites

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The development of an environmentally safe soybean-based adhesive with desired adhesion properties and technological applicabilities, but low cost, still remains a challenge. In this study, a facile and clean strategy was developed to improve the adhesion properties and technological applicabilities and to reduce the cost of a soybean meal flour (SMF)-based adhesive through organic-inorganic hybridization with kaolin powder. The effects of kaolin hybridization and kaolin content on the structure and properties of the SMF-based adhesive were revealed. The improved water resistance of the adhesion was attributed to the effective organic-inorganic hybridization of the SMF adhesive with a uniform distribution of kaolin, the hydrogen bonding interactions between the intercalated SMF with the partial kaolin interlayers, and the chemical reaction between the crosslinker and kaolin. In addition, kaolin significantly decreased the viscosity and alleviated the shear thinning characteristics of the SMF adhesive because the kaolin-kaolin intermolecular interactions were weaker than the interactions between the SMF chains. Hydrogen bonding interactions between the SMF chains and the kaolin particles were observed, and the water absorption and bonded water by kaolin were greatly reduced. The most preferable kaolin content in the SMF adhesive was 30%, which decreased the adhesive cost by 11.4%. Thus, this novel strategy could effectively expand the applications of SMF-based adhesives in environmentally friendly wood composites by replacing formaldehyde-based synthetic resins that release free formaldehyde.

ce:section.ce:para: Due to the desired adhesion strength, acceptable water resistance, and good technological applicability, formaldehyde-based synthetic adhesives, such as urea-formaldehyde, melamine-formaldehyde, and phenol-formaldehyde, are predominantly used in the production of wood composites, such as plywood, particleboard, medium density fiber board, hipboard, and oriented standard board [1,2]. However, these adhesives not only are derived from nonrenewable fossil resources but also release harmful free formaldehyde during their production, storage, transportation, and use [3]. Due to the growing environmental concerns and increasingly strict environmental legislation, the continued depletion of nonsustainable fossil fuel reserves, and the uncertainty in future crude oil prices, there is strong academic and industrial interest in the development of biobased adhesives and biocomposites from renewable, nontoxic, and sustainable bioresources [4–6]. Soybean meal flour (SMF), a by-product from soybean oil production, is abundant and has acceptable protein content. Therefore, SMF is an ideal raw material for biobased adhesives to replace traditional petroleum-based synthetic adhesives [7]. However, traditional soybean-based adhesives suffer from poor water resistance in adhesion and high viscosity, and they are also relatively more expensive than the dominant urea-formaldehyde adhesives. These factors limit the application of SMF-based adhesives in the wood composite industry.

There have been many attempts to improve the water resistance and bond strength of soybean-based adhesives, including physical, chemical, and biological modifications. Among these modifications, alkali [8], urea [9], sodium dodecyl sulfate [10], and thermal-acid treatments [11] have been found to unfold the compact spherical structure of soybean protein and expose the buried hydrophobic groups, leading to improved water resistance in the soybean-based adhesive. In addition, crosslinkers such as polyamide-epichlorohydrin [4,11,12], polyisocyanate [13], and epoxy resin [14–16] could effectively improve the water resistance of soybean-based adhesives because these crosslinkers react with groups in the soybean protein to form an insoluble three-dimensional network structure. Among these crosslinkers, the crosslinker polyamide-epichlorohydrin with reactive azetidinium groups exhibited good compatibility and crosslinking efficiency towards soybean protein and has been used commercially to prepare soybean adhesives with desired water resistance for wood composites [4,11]. However, the cost of commercialized polyamide-epichlorohydrin-SMF adhesives is approximately 15–40% higher than the cost of the urea-formaldehyde adhesive.

Organic-inorganic hybridization of polymer materials with inorganic substances has been widely reported, resulting in effective improvements in many aspects such as mechanical properties, thermal stability and flammability [17]. Recently, some inorganic nanoparticles such as montmorillonite and attapulgite have also been used to modify soybean protein-based adhesives. These nanoparticles were found to effectively improve the adhesion properties, water resistance, and thermal stability due to their unique nanoscale structure, high particle aspect ratio, and the formation of inorganic-organic hybrids [18–20]. Although nanoscale montmorillonite has been reported to be a promising modifier to improve the adhesion properties of soybean protein-based adhesives, its cost is too high for commercialization. In addition, these inorganic nanoparticles sharply increase the viscosity of the adhesive even when added in small amounts (commonly less than 5 wt % of the adhesive) [13,18–21] because of the strong absorption of free water by the nanoparticle and significant polymer-nanoparticle interaction resulting from their high surface energy. A high viscosity always lowers the wettability and hinders uniform spreading of the modified adhesive.

The desired inorganic modifiers in adhesives should be sufficiently low in cost while capable of being added in large quantities. To this end, we performed preliminary tests on fine inorganic powders with costs ranging from 150 to 300 USD/ton, and only kaolin could meet the above criteria. Kaolin costs approximately 210 USD/ton (while SMF made from white flakes is approximately 600 USD/ton) and could be added to SMF at a level above 45 wt %. Kaolin, also known as porcelain stone, is a collection of hydrous aluminosilicates composed of a variety of minerals. Its main component is kaolinite with a general formula of Al2Si2O5(OH)4 or 2SiO2·Al2O3·2H2O. Kaolin has a typical 1:1 layered silicate structure, and the basic structural units consist of a periodical arrangement of a double-layer structure of a tetrahedral silica (SiO4) layer and an octahedral alumina [AlO2(OH)4] layer. The apical oxygen atoms from the silica layer are shared with aluminum atoms from the adjacent alumina layer, by which the adjacent layers are bonded via van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds to form a dioctahedral structure [22]. As an important layered silicate mineral, kaolin has a highly regular sheet structure, good plasticity, easy dispersibility, high whiteness, large specific surface area, and excellent electrical insulation [23,24]. Therefore, kaolin is widely used in industries such as electronics, ceramics, rubber, plastics, paper making, petrochemicals, and coatings because of its strong orientation in polymers.

In the current study, fine kaolin powder was used to modify the SMF-based adhesive via organic-inorganic hybridization with attempts to effectively decrease the material cost while retaining the desired applicability, adhesion strength, and water resistance. Unlike previously reported inorganic nanoparticles which were added at 0.05–5 wt %, kaolin could be added at a much larger amount (15–75 wt %). The mechanism and effects of kaolin hybridization on the structure and properties of SMF-based adhesives were comprehensively investigated by means of FTIR, XPS, XRD, TGA, SEM, rheological analyses and plywood evaluation. These results should provide useful information for clean production and further R&D of SMF-based materials and adhesives.

SMF (average protein content 53.4%, water content 6.7% and particle size passed 160-mesh sieve) was purchased from Harbin High-Tech Soybean Food Co., Ltd. Kaolin powder (1250 mesh) was obtained from Tianjin Kermel Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd, China. Aqueous epichlorohydrin-modified polyamide (EMPA, also called polyamide-epichlorohydrin) solution was synthesized in our laboratory utilizing diethylenetriamine, adipic acid, and epichlorohydrin. The prepared solution had a solid content of 12.0%, a pH of 2.7, and a viscosity of 83.7 mPa∙s at 25 °C. Birch veneers with dimensions of 350 mm × 350 mm and moisture content of 6–8% were provided by Weihe Fulin Wood Factory, China.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of kaolin-hybridized SMF adhesives, viscosity measurement, and cured sample preparation
ce:section.ce:para: Fine kaolin powder was mechanically mixed with SMF at different ratios (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75 wt % kaolin in the mixture). A corresponding series of kaolin-modified SMF adhesives was prepared by mechanically blending 35 parts of kaolin-SMF mixture with 100 parts of EMPA solution by mass at room temperature, until no particle clusters were observed (approximately 10 min). The prepared adhesives were labeled as Kaolin0, Kaolin15, Kaolin30, Kaolin45, Kaolin60, and Kaolin75, respectively.

The viscosity of the adhesive was determined after soaking in a water bath thermostated at 25 °C for more than 30 min, using a Brookfield DV-II + PRO viscometer at the rotating speed of 10 rpm. The viscosity of a sample without the soybean meal flour (i.e., 35 parts of kaolin mixed with 100 parts of EMPA solution) was also determined.

Cured adhesive samples were produced by placing approximately 25 g of kaolin-hybridized SMF liquid adhesive in a polytetrafluoroethylene container, and then curing at 120 °C for 4 h. After cooling to room temperature, the cured sample was ground into fine powder and passed through a 160-mesh sieve before characterization tests using X-ray diffraction (XRD), FTIR, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).

Three-ply plywood was fabricated with a liquid adhesive loading of 200 g/m2 for a single glueline, by coating the adhesive onto both surfaces of the core veneer (1.6 mm thick). This core veneer was sandwiched between two uncoated face veneers (1.6 mm thick) by hand, with the grains of adjacent veneers vertical to each other. Then, the sample was cold-pressed at 1.1 MPa at room temperature for 1 h, followed by hot pressing at 120 °C and 1.3 MPa for 4.5 min. Then, the panels were stored openly under an ambient environment for at least 24 h before testing. From each prepared panel, 30 specimens with a bond area of 25 mm × 25 mm were cut out to determine the bond strength and water resistance. Specifically, 10 specimens were used to determine each of the three properties: the dry bond strength, soaked wet bond strength, and cycled wet bond strength. The tests were conducted according to the commercial standard JIS K6806-2003 using a tensile testing machine with a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min. For the soaked wet bond strength test, the specimen was soaked in 63 ± 2 °C water for 3 h and then cooled at room temperature for 10 min before measuring the shear tensile strength. For the cycled wet bond strength test, the specimen was subjected to a boiling-dry-boiling hygrothermal treatment (4 h of boiling, 20 h of oven-drying at 63 ± 2 °C, and then another 4 h of boiling) before measurement of the shear tensile strength in the wet state at room temperature.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of boiling-water-insoluble content of cured kaolin-EMPA mixture
ce:section.ce:para: To assess the extent of chemical bonding between kaolin and the crosslinker EMPA, various kaolin-EMPA mixtures with the same kaolin/EMPA mass ratio as the SMF-kaolin-EMPA mixtures (adhesives) were also cured and then ground per the procedures described in Section 2.2. Then, approximately 1.0 g of each cured powder sample (W0, accurate to 0.0001 g) and 100.0 g of distilled water were added into a 250-mL conical flask, and then the mixture was stirred and kept boiling for 4 h to dissolve the noncrosslinked components. The boiled dispersion was cooled to room temperature and filtered, and the residue was rinsed twice with 50 mL of distilled water. The residue on the glass-filter paper (W1, accurate to 0.0001 g) was oven-dried at 120 °C to a constant weight (W2, accurate to 0.0001 g). The water-insoluble content was defined as the mass percentage of the insoluble component, [(W2-W1)/W0] × 100%. The boiling-water-insoluble content of kaolin alone was also determined as a control. All samples were tested in triplicate. Assuming that kaolin does not react with EMPA, the theoretical boiling-water-insoluble content could be calculated using the values for kaolin alone (ICK) and cured EMPA alone (ICEMPA), according to their masses (MK and MEMPA) contained in various kaolin-solid EMPA mixtures as (MK × ICK + MEMPA × ICEMPA)/(MK + MEMPA) × 100%.

XRD analysis can provide information about the crystallinity or disorder of kaolin in the cured SMF adhesive, in terms of the Aparicio-Galan-Ferrell index (AGFI) according to the literature [25]. Fine powders of cured SMF adhesives were analyzed in a D/max-2200 diffractometer (Rigaku International Corporation, Tokyo, Japan). X-ray radiation was generated from a Cu-Kα source at an accelerating voltage of 40 kV and a current of 30 mA. The diffraction data were collected from 5° to 50° with a step interval of 0.02°.

To confirm the intercalation of EMPA and/or SMF in kaolin, a reference sample (labeled as Kaolin30-comp) was prepared by evenly mixing 30% fine kaolin powder with fine powder of cured adhesive Kaolin0 (i.e., mixture of SMF and EMPA solution without kaolin) in the dry state at room temperature. This reference sample was also analyzed by XRD.

Each powder sample of pure kaolin, SMF, Kaolin0, Kaolin30, and Kaolin30-comp was mixed with potassium bromide crystals at a weight ratio of approximately 1/150 and then thoroughly ground. The ground mixture was pressed in a special mold to obtain a tablet sample for FTIR analysis. The spectra were recorded from 4000 to 400 cm−1 using a Spectrum One FTIR spectrophotometer (Nicolet Co., USA). Each sample was scanned 32 times with a resolution of 4 cm−1. The IR peak at approximately 1630 cm−1, which represents the C=O stretching (amide I) vibration, was selected as an internal standard. The spectrum was subjected to baseline correction and concentration correction using the software OMNIC E.S.P. (Nicolet Co., USA).

The cured adhesive samples (Kaolin0, Kaolin15, Kaolin30, Kaolin45, and Kaolin60) and pure kaolin were separately subjected to TGA analysis using a Netzsch 209 F3 TGA instrument from room temperature to 600 °C at a heating rate 10 °C/min under a nitrogen purge of 25 mL/min.

To investigate the evaporating rate of free water, liquid Kaolin0 adhesive and the kaolin dispersion in EMPA solution (Kaolin100) were placed between filter papers. Then, the sample was squeezed by hand to remove partial free water until no more moisture came out. The squeezed sample was immediately subjected to TGA analysis using the Netzsch 209 F3 TGA instrument from room temperature (30 °C) to 110 °C at a heating rate of 1 °C/min under a nitrogen purge of 25 mL/min. Meanwhile, the water content in each squeezed sample for TGA analysis was determined by oven drying at 103 ± 2 °C for 6 h.

To investigate the effect of kaolin addition on the permeability of SMF adhesive within wood, XPS analysis was employed to determine the elemental concentrations of C, O, and N in various depths/layers of wood after spreading the adhesive on top at 200 g/m2. The XPS sample was prepared as follows.
a)
A 2.4 mm-thick birch veneer was cut down to 200 mm × 200 mm, and then both its surfaces were sanded to produce a thickness of 2.00 ± 0.01 mm with micrometer calipers.
b)
Kaolin-modified liquid SMF adhesive was spread on the clean and sanded surface.
c)
A 0.5 mm-thick polytetrafluoroethylene film was placed atop the adhesive, followed by cold pressing at 1.1 MPa for 1 h and hot pressing at 120 °C and 1.3 MPa for 4 min in sequence.
d)
The hot-pressed veneer panel was cut into 200 mm × 20 mm strips after cooling down, and the polytetrafluoroethylene film was removed.
e)
A strip without deformation was selected and tightly fixed on a flat table.
f)
The upper surface of the fixed strip was polished with 300-mesh sandpaper carefully, while the polishing surface was kept parallel to the table face as it was monitored with a spiral micrometer.
g)
Powder polished from the original surface at 0.02 mm depth was collected and labeled, while that below 0.03 mm in panel depth was discarded.
h)
Step g) was repeated until approximately 0.4 mm of the veneer was polished away from the coated surface.

For each SMF adhesive, a total of 8 polished powder samples were collected for XPS analysis using a Kα X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with monochromatic Al-Kα radiation at 100 W. High-energy photoemission spectra were recorded using a pass energy of 50 eV and a resolution of 0.1 eV. The XPS peak areas of C1s, O1s, and N1s were calculated to represent the respective concentration of elements C, O, and N in the sample, by calibrating the peak area with the PHI sensitivity factor of the element (C = 0.296, O = 0.711, N = 0.477). The depth of the XPS sample from adhesive-coated veneer surface was represented by the averaged depth. For instance, the depth of the first layer, located between 0.00 and 0.02 mm away from the surface, was represented as 0.01 mm.

Prior to the SEM analysis, an amount of liquid SMF-based adhesive hybridized with given kaolin content was placed in a Teflon pool. Then, the pool was placed in an oven at 120 ± 2 °C for 4 h to obtain a cured adhesive film that was approximately 1.5 mm thick. The adhesive film was fractured at ambient condition, and the fractured surface was examined with a QUANTA-200 SEM instrument (FEI Co., USA) after being coated with approximately 10–20 nm of gold.

The dynamic viscosity of each SMF-based adhesive was measured by an Ar 2000ex rheometer (TA Instruments-Waters LLC, USA) with a parallel plate (25 mm plate diameter) at 25 °C. The distance between the cone and plate was set at 1500 μm, and the shear rate was in the range of 10–100 s−1.

According to the commercial standard JIS K 6806-2003, the wet bond strength after soaking in 63 °C water for 3 h represents the moisture resistance of plywood used for indoor products with strength value exceeding 0.98 MPa on average. Meanwhile, the wet bond strength after boiling-dry-boiling hygrothermal treatment represents the water or weather resistance of plywood used outdoors or in structural products that also have strength values more than 0.98 MPa on average. Test results in Fig. 1 indicate that the plywood bonded with Kaolin0 (without kaolin addition) had a soaking wet bond strength of 1.18 MPa and a cycled wet bond strength of 0.87 MPa, exhibiting the desired moisture resistance for indoor products but insufficient water or weather resistance for outdoors or structural products. The addition of kaolin to the adhesives improved the soaked wet bond strength and cycled wet bond strength, and these strength values first decreased with the kaolin content and then gradually increased from 15% to 60%. Kaolin30 has the highest soaked wet bond strength (1.41 MPa) and the highest cycled wet bond strength (1.16 MPa), both of which exceed the requirements for indoor and outdoor uses (0.98 MPa) with significance at p-values < 0.05 according to the one-way ANOVA analysis. However, further increasing the kaolin level to 75% dramatically decreased both values, to even lower than those of Kaolin0. This decreased bond strength was due to excessive amounts of kaolin.

The kaolin applied in this study is an inorganic fine powder that does not dissolve well. However, the kaolin can evenly disperse in the aqueous SMF-EMPA system to form a homogeneous adhesive without particle clusters under mechanical stirring due to the amphiphilic structure of soybean protein as an emulsifier [26]. In the microstructures observed by SEM in Fig. 2 , SMF adhesive films with 0–30% kaolin (Fig. 2a, b and c) had compact and uniform fractured surfaces without visible kaolin particles, indicating that kaolin was uniformly distributed in the adhesive system. In the SMF-EMPA-kaolin system, the strong kaolin particles act as reinforcement to effectively disperse the stress. Meanwhile, kaolin hybridization forms a compact adhesive layer that inhibits the water penetration, thereby increasing the water resistance and bond strength of the modified adhesive. Further increase of the kaolin level from 45% to 75% causes the kaolin particles to aggregate gradually as shown by Fig. 2d, e and f, respectively, due to insufficient emulsification or discontinuous embedding of kaolin particles in SMF. As a result, more and more pores were formed in the SMF adhesive films with kaolin content from 45% to 75%. In the film of Kaolin75, kaolin particles obviously aggregated to form abundant pores, and the polymer phase of the adhesive became discontinuous, preventing effective stress dispersion and allowing water to penetrate the adhesive layer. Thus, both the water resistance and bond strength decreased.

The intercalating interaction between kaolin and SMF adhesive was also investigated by FTIR analysis. As shown in Fig. 5 A, samples of SMF and Kaolin0 had an IR absorption peak at approximately 1048 cm−1 assigned to the C-O stretching of soybean protein and carbohydrates [28]. Meanwhile, kaolin alone had the characteristic absorption bands at approximately 1060 cm−1 corresponding to the Si-O in-plane stretching [27], and EMPA alone had the characteristic absorption bands at approximately 1630, 1520 and 1240 cm−1 corresponding to the C=O stretching, N-H bending and C-N/N-H stretching, respectively. Due to the formation of new hydrogen bonds between the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group with the amino group in SMF adhesive or the oxygen atom of Si-O in kaolin (as illustrated in Fig. 4), the absorption peak of Kaolin30 at approximately 1048–1060 cm−1 was obviously weaker than the absorption peak of Kaolin30-comp, but stronger than the absorption peak of Kaolin0. The formation of chemical bonds between kaolin and EMPA as shown by Eq. (b) in Fig. 6 reduced the reactions of EMPA with SMF (crosslinking reaction) and EMPA (self-crosslinking as shown by Eq. (a) in Fig. 6), resulting in fewer C-N bonds as indicated by the lowest absorption peak of Kaolin30 at approximately 1240 cm−1 compared with EMPA alone, Kaolin0 and Kaolin30-comp. TGA analysis in Fig. 5B shows that the weight-loss stages for Kaolin0 at approximately 200 °C and 420 °C almost or completely disappeared in the adhesives with added kaolin, further indicating the formation of new interactions such as hydrogen bonds and chemical bonds in the kaolin-hybridized SMF adhesives which affected their thermal degradation modes.

The boiling-water-insoluble content is correlated positively with the crosslinking degree of cured adhesive, and stronger crosslinking usually means improved water resistance [4,29]. To verify whether the intercalated SMF adhesive could react with kaolin interlayers, the boiling-water-insoluble contents of various samples were measured. Kaolin itself has a boiling-water-insoluble content of 84.01% due to its poor solubility, while the boiling-water-insoluble content of cured EMPA alone is also high (81.17%) because of the self-crosslinking as shown by Eq. (a) in Fig. 6. If EMPA does not react with kaolin, then the cured kaolin-EMPA mixture would have a boiling-water-insoluble content close to its theoretical value. However, according to the data in Fig. 6, when the kaolin content in the kaolin-EMPA mixtures was gradually increased from 15% to 75%, the boiling-water-insoluble content exceeded the corresponding theoretical values by 5.4–7.6% (percentage difference), implying that the EMPA could react with kaolin as shown by Eq. (b) in Fig. 6, according to the report that found that the azetidinium ring of EMPA is analogous to an epoxide and reacts with the hydroxyl groups [30]. The formed chemical bonds (as shown by solid lines between kaolin and EMPA in Fig. 4) could strengthen the interactions between kaolin and SMF adhesive and thus help to improve the water resistance of kaolin-hybridized SMF adhesives.

In addition to the good bond strength and water resistance, a wood adhesive should have good technological applicability and low cost. Viscosity is the most important parameter for the technological applicability of an adhesive, since it affects the solid content, the tack properties, the spreading properties, and the wettability of the adhesive [2,31]. A proper viscosity allows SMF-based adhesives to achieve higher solid content with less water introduced to disperse the SMF and, therefore, reduce the hot-pressing time of wood composites to remove the water. In addition, a proper viscosity allows the adhesive to be easily and evenly spread onto the wood surface and sufficiently wet the wood substrate, which will be beneficial for tack properties and adhesion properties by promoting the interfacial adhesion. The apparent viscosity of liquid SMF adhesives with various kaolin content is shown in Fig. 7 A. The control adhesive Kaolin0 without kaolin had an extremely high viscosity of 16700 mPa∙s and a notable fluid accumulation when it was poured (shown in pink frame in the photographs in Fig. 7), mainly due to the high molecular weight of the SMF component, as well as the presence of abundant intermolecular interactions within the adhesive. Interactions such as chain entanglement of SMF components and hydrogen bonds were easily destroyed at an increased shear rate, resulting in notable shear thinning behavior of Kaolin0 (Fig. 7B).

After kaolin alone was evenly dispersed in the EMPA solution, this dispersion (Kaolin100) had a much lower viscosity (3415 mPa∙s) than the adhesive without kaolin (Kaolin0, 16700 mPa∙s) because the interactions (such as entanglement and hydrogen bonds) between SMF chains are much stronger than the interactions between kaolin-kaolin particles. This level of interaction is beneficial to the formation of SMF chain-kaolin interactions including intercalation by reducing the free energy of SMF adhesive, as illustrated in Fig. 4, which weakens the strong adsorption between the SMF chains. The viscosity of a solution is well known to increase with its concentration. The squeezed fresh Kaolin100 sample had a much lower water content (12.9 wt %) than squeezed fresh Kaolin0 (52.5 wt %), indicating that kaolin absorbed much less water than SMF in the liquid SMF adhesive. In addition, TGA analysis results in Fig. 8 indicate that the water absorbed by kaolin was mainly free water that was evaporated between 50 and 90 °C, while the water absorbed by SMF was bonded water that was difficult to evaporate below 100 °C. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that adding kaolin to SMF could reduce both the water absorption and bonded water by SMF and increase the amount of free water in the liquid adhesive system. As a result, the viscosity and fluid accumulation of SMF adhesive decreased gradually when the kaolin content increased from 0% to 75%. Therefore, after adding a proper amount of kaolin, the decreased viscosity not only effectively improved the adhesive fluidity (i.e., reduced the fluid accumulation shown in the photographs of Fig. 7) and its penetration (slower N/(C + O) decrease with depth in wood, Fig. 9 B) but also reduced the viscosity variation of the adhesive during the spreading process when producing wood composites (i.e., a slower viscosity decrease with shear rate in Fig. 7B).

However, if there is too much kaolin (75%, for instance), the very low viscosity of the adhesive could lead to overpenetration into the porous wood substrate, as evidenced by the adhesive penetration analysis. Because the wood itself contains mostly C, H, and O elements with negligible N content, the N1s peak in the XPS curves (Fig. 9A) is attributed to soybean protein and EMPA in the SMF adhesive. Therefore, the ratio of elemental concentration N/(C + O) reflects the adhesive concentration at the various depths of the glueline, which decreases with the depth as shown in Fig. 9B. Compared with Kaolin0 and Kaolin30, Kaolin75 with a lower viscosity could better penetrate the wood, as evidenced by the smallest slope of N/(C + O) value against glueline depth as well as the lowest N/(C + O) value at surface layer (depth = 0.01 mm) and highest value in the deepest layer (0.36 mm). For Kaolin75, the N/(C + O) value at the surface layer is 34.9% and 25.2% lower than the N/(C + O) values of Kaolin0 and Kaolin30, respectively, indicating that more liquid Kaolin75 penetrated the wood than Kaolin30, which was in turn more than Kaolin0.

In addition, SEM observation in Fig. 2f indicated that excessive kaolin addition breaks the continuous polymer matrix of SMF, preventing effective stress transfer [32]. The discontinuous polymer matrix and the lack of adhesion at the interface are responsible for the lowest dry bond strength, soaked wet bond strength, and cycled wet bond strength when the adhesive contains the largest amount of kaolin (Fig. 1). Considering the bond property, technological applicability, and microstructure, we determined that the optimal kaolin content in the SMF adhesive for indoor use was 45%, since the measured soaked wet bond strength was 39.8% more than the required value according to the commercial standard. At this ratio, Kaolin45 would have a cost 18.2% lower than the cost of Kaolin0. Meanwhile, the most preferable kaolin content for outdoor use was 30%, which corresponds to the best cycled wet bond strength (33.3% more than that without Kaolin hybridization, Kaolin0), while reducing the adhesive cost by 11.4%.

An easy and green strategy for producing environmentally safe SMF-based adhesives was developed through organic-inorganic hybridization with low-cost kaolin, which could improve the bond properties and technological applicabilities of SMF-based wood adhesives and reduce the adhesive cost by 11.4%–18.2%. A proper level of kaolin improves the water resistance of the adhesive due to the uniform distribution of kaolin particles in the adhesive, the intercalation of EMPA and/or SMF chains within partial kaolin interlayers, and the chemical reaction between EMPA and kaolin, all of which strengthen the interactions between kaolin and the SMF adhesive. Further, the kaolin-modified SMF adhesive has improved technological applicability in terms of lower viscosity and less shear thinning characteristic because the fine kaolin powder can weaken the adsorption and entanglements between the SMF chains. However, excessive kaolin addition could significantly harm the adhesion properties of the SMF adhesives, and the most preferable kaolin level was determined to be 30%.
